chapter.title: Introduction
chapter.para: This document provides information about spectra saved to HDF5 formatted files. Starting with SpecTcl 7.0-005, swrite and sread support -format hdf5 which allows spectrum to be written to HDF5 formatted files. HDF5 iteslf is beyond the scope of this document. For information about HDF5, see .

This document is intended for people who want to make use of spectra stored in HDF5 files outside of SpecTcl. A specTcl installation will have this document in html format in $SPECTCLHOME/share/hdf5/index.html where $SPECTCLHOME is the top level of the installation directory.

SpecTcl provies a low level library libhdfReader that contains a C++ class that can extract information about and the contents of spectra that are stored in those files. The remainder of this document is organized as follows:

listitem.para: Describes the compilation and link options you'll need to supply to use this library in your programs.

Works through an example program that makes use of the library. This program, and the sample data file are available in $SPECTCLHOME/share/hdf5example where $SPECTCLHOME is the top level directory of a SpecTcl instalation.
Provides a class reference.
Provides information that describes how the HDF5 is structured. You will need to have a basic understanding of the objects that can live in an HDF5 file to understand this information.

chapter.para: This section works through a simple program that uses the hdfReader API. The program iself is installed in $SPECTCLHOME/share/hdf5example/listample.cpp. It opens a sample HDF5 data file from its working directory and exercises the HDF5 spectrum API. example.title: Sample libhdfReader program

chapter.para: In the discussion below, refer to the numbered callouts in the example above for the corresponding code.

callout.para: Inludes the header that defines the hdfSpectrumReader class which provides support for reading the SpecTcl swrite -format hdf5 .

Creating an instance of the hdfSpectruReader, opens the file path passed to it as an HDF5 file readonly. When the object is destroyed, its destructor will close that HDF5 file. The methods of this object will provide access to the objects that are stored in the file.

The objects in the HDF5 file are associated with spectra. Each spectrum stored in the file has a name, the name of that spectrum in SpecTcl if swrite -format hdf5 was used to write it. The listSpectra method returns a vector of strings that provide the names of the spectra that are stored in the file.

The program is going to iterate over the names gotten from listSpectra and operate on each spectrum in turn. If you are not familiar with this form of the C++ for loop, it iterates over all elements of a collection that supports generating iterators with betin and end and for each iteration, in this case, the variable n is assigned to one of the values in the collection.
For a more complete description of this so-called range-based for loop you can see

Each SpecTcl spectrum has a channel data type. The dataType method takes a spectrum name for a spetrum that is in the file and provides it's data type string. For SpecTcl this is a string containing one of:

listitem.para: uint32_t data.
uint16_t data.
uint8_t data.

callout.para:
While SpecTcl provides 1-D and 2-D spectra, its spectra also describe how events increment them in a very rich way. The spectrumType takes a spectrum name and returns a string that defines the spectrum type. For a list of spectrum types supported by SpecTcl, see the spectrum reference in the
SpecTcl Command reference

Since SpecTcl spectra are fundamentally 1-D or 2-D data, they may have one or two axis definitions. An axis definition describes a mapping between parameter space and the bins of a spectrum. The getXaxis returns the X axis definition of a the spectrum whose name was passed to it. All Spectra have an X axis definition. The axis definition is returned as a struct (hdf5SpectrumReader::AxisDefinition). With the following fields:

listitem.para: The low limit of parameter space represented by the axis.
The high limit of parameter space represented by the axis.
The number of bins on the axis.

callout.para: While all spectra have an X axis, only those that are fundamentally 2-d have Y axes. The hasYAxis when passed the name of a spectrum returns true if that spectrum has a Y axis, false if not.
If a specturm has a Y axis it is safe to invoke getYaxis which returns its axis definition.

The getParameters retuns a list of the names of parameters for the spectrum, but see, however getYParameters below. In many cases, a 2-d spectrum's parameter can be described by a single list, for example, a simple 2-d spectrum's X parameter will be the first in the list and the Y parameter, the second.

Some spectrum types are not unambiguosyl defined by a single list of parameters. For example the Gamma Deluxe (gd) spectrum has a set of X axis parameters and a set of Y axis parameters and increments for any pair of those that are present. It is best described by a pair of parameter lists. The hasYparameters returns true if there is a second parameter list for the spectrum. That second set of parameters is returned from getYParameters.

All SpecTcl spectra have a gate applied to it. When created, the spectrum's gate is called -TRUE- and is true for all events. Subsequently, more intereting gates can be created and applied to the spectrum. The getGate returns the name of the gate that was applied to the spetrum at the time the file was created.

Spectra can have arbitrary metadata associated with them. Spectrum metadata is simply a set of name/value pairs where both the name and the value are strings. The getMetadata returns the metadata for a spectrum as an std::vector<std::pair<std::string std::string>>. Each pair is a metadata item. the first element of the pair is the name of that metadata item and the second element of the pair is the value of that metadata item.

Finally, and maybe most importantly, the contents of the spectra can be retrieved from file. The result of a call to getContents is a pointer to dynmamically allocated storage which contains the contents of the spectrum saved to file. Note how the code blow the call to getContents uses the data type string returned from dataType to create the appropriate pointer type. In our simple example, we just then free the storage allocated by getContents.
What you do with spectrum contents is so application specific that we leave that completely up to you.

chapter.title: class hdfSpectrumReader reference
chapter.para: This section contains a comprehensive reference for the hdfSpectrumReader class that forms the sole public export of the libhdfReader library.

refsect1.title: DESCRIPTION
refsect1.para: The hdfSpectrumReader class provides low level access to SpecTcl spectrum data that the swrite -format hdf5... wrote. Its use is rather simple. Create an object to open a file and then invoke the methods to get data from it.

The key point is that spectra have names and that associated with each spectrum is data of various sorts. These are retrieved via the methods described below by supplying the name of the spectrum they are associated with.

listitem.para: The constructor opens the HDF5 file specified by path. While HDF5's low level library, presumably ensures that the file is an HDF5 file, we do no checkes to ensure its contents are compatible with our functionality.

HDF5 error reporting is managed by the caller. By default, errors will printout verbose tracebacks that are hard to decipher. You can change this behavior by invoking H5::Exception::dontPrint() and catching exceptions thrown by HDF5. For more information on HDF5 exceptions refer to the documentation of the HDF5 Exception class. Expanding the inheritance diagram will also show the set of derived classes.
Returns a vector of strings containing the names of the spectra that are in the file.

Note that spectra are top level HDF5 groups in the file. This method just lists the names of the top level groups. If, after the file is initially written, your applications add to the set of top level groups, it is the responsibility of your code to tell the differnce between the names in this vector that actually are spectra and which are not.

Returns the string form of the SpecTcl spectrum type of the spectrum named by name. The list of valid spectru, types and their meanings is descsribed in the reference to the SpecTcl spectrum in the
SpecTcl command reference
Returns a string that describes the bin data type for the spectrum name. THis is one of long for uint32_t, short for uint16_t, and bytes for uint8_t

SpecTcl spectra are fundamentally 1D or 2D. This method returns true if the spectrum name is a 2D spectrum. Note that a SpecTcl spectrum can be thought of as data with type and shape and a strategy for incrementing bins in the shaped data given an event. hasYAxis adresses the shape of the spectrum data.
Returns the definition of the X axis for the spectrum. All spectra have an X axis. See for information about the hdfSpectrumRader::AxisDefinition struct.
Returns the Y axis definition for the 2-d spectrum: name. This method will thrown an HDF5 exception if hasYAxis for this spectrum returned false.

Returns the name of the gate applied to the spectrum when the file was written. In SpecTcl, every spectrum has a gate applied to it. When created, the pre-defined gate -TRUE- is applied. -TRUE- is a gate that is true for every event.
After a spectrum has been created, a more interesting gate may be applied to it at a later time.
For spectra which only need one list of parameters to unambiguously konw how to increment, this returns that list for name For spectra that require 2 lists of parameters, this returns the X list.

For most spectra, a single list of parameters suffices to determine how the spectrum is incremented. For example a 2-d spectrum (type 2), requires an X and Y parameter. WHere the X parameter is the first one and the Y the second one.
Returns true if the deifnition of the spectrum name cannot be determined unambiguously from a single list of parameters.
Returns the second list of parameters for spectra (name) that need it. If hasYparameters returned false an exception is raised from HDF5.

Returns the metadata associated with spectrum name Spectrum metadata consists of a list of name/value pairs where both the name and values are strings. The metadata are returned a a vector of pairs. The first element of each pair is the name of a metadata item and the second, that metadata item's value.

Returns a pointer to dynamically allocated storage that contains the contents of spectrum name read from file. The interpretation of this soup of storage depends on the actual data type and the shape of the spectrum. The sample code shows how to interpret the data type. You can inspect the axis definition(s) to understand the shape of the storage.

refsect1.title: DATA TYPES
refsect1.para: The class hdfSpectrumReader has a single public data type: AxisDefinition. As its name implies, this is a struct that defines the mapping of parameter space onto the bins of an axis of a spectrum. It also, therefore, describes the shape of one axis of spectrum storage.

listitem.para: The parameter space low limit of the axis.
The parameter space high limit of the axis.
The number of histogram bins on this axis.

appendix.title: HDF5 file data structure
appendix.para: HDF5 files files can represent data in many ways. This section describes how the files containing SpecTcl spectrum data written with swrite -format hdf5 are structured. To understand this appendix you will need to understand several basic HDF5 concepts:

listitem.para: Groups: A group can be thought of as a directory like object. It is a container for other objects, including other groups if the file designer so chooses.
DataSets: A data set is an object that contains bulk data. A data set is effectively a multi-dimensional array of some type of data.
Attributes: Attributes are small chunks of data that are associated with other object, including groups and data sets
Files: A file is exactly that a file containing HDF5 objects. Files are also a Root Group in the sense that any operation you can perform on a group can be performed on a file object in the API.

appendix.para: You can find complete information about HDF5 files and the various APIs that are available at .

Armed with this understanding of HDF5 files, we can proceed with a description of the objects in spectrum files and their relationships. The goal of this design is to capture the contents of one or more spectra in a way that allows the spectrum and its contents to be restored within SpecTcl. As such, the contents of a spectrum, while typically by far the largest volume of data in a file is only one of many different bits of data.

HDF5 files can hold several spectra. Therefore, each spectrum is data attached to a top level group in the HDF5 file. The name of that group is the name of the spectrum. For example, a spectrum named raw.00 will result in a group that is a child of the root group (the file) named raw.00. I'll refer to this as a spectrum group.

The spectrum group has a pair of attributes:
spectrumtype
Contains a text string that is the SpecTcl spectrum type. See the SpecTcl command reference documentation of the spectrum for an enumeration of the valid strings and their meanings.
datatype
Contains a string that identifies the data type of bins in the spectrum. This can be any of long for uint32_t, word for uint16_t or byte for uint8_t.

The most important data set owned by the spectrum group is contents It containst he bulk data of the spectrum (the bins). HDF5 allows for data type mapping/translation between file datat types and native data types. For the contents data set, this mapping is determined by the data type (stored as an attribute of the spectrum group).

listitem.para: This maps PredType::NATIVE_UINT32 to a file data type of PredType::STD_U32LE
This maps PredType::NATIVE_UINT16 to a file data type of PredType::STD_U16LE.
This maps PredType::NATIVE_UINT8 to PredType::STD_UINT8LE

appendix.para: See the HDF5 PredType reference for more information about those type identifying classes.
The dimensionality and dimensions of the actual data space depends are taken from the spectrum itself.
The contents data set has several attributes:

listitem.para: Contains three PredType::IEEE_F32LE values that are, in order, the X axis parameter space low limit, the X axis parameter space high limit and the number of X axis bins.
The same information as Xaxis but for the spectrum Y axis, if it has one. If the spectrum has no Y axis, this attribute will not be present.

Contains the name of the gate that was applied to the spectrum when it was written. Note that all SpecTcl spectra have gates. Spectra that are ungated actually have a gate applied to them named -TRUE- which is a predefined SpecTcl gate that is always true for all events.

appendix.para: In addition to the contents data set there are three other data sets under the spectrum group. These can be used by SpecTcl to reconstruct the spectrum as an actively incrementing spectrum or provide documentation to you of what the spectrum is.

formalpara.title: The xparamters dataset
formalpara.para: If there are X parameters, this data set contains an ordered list of strings (StrType(PredType::C_S1, H5T_VARIABLE)) that are the list of X parameter names. See the StrType class reference for more about this data type.

formalpara.title: The yparameters dataset
formalpara.para: If the spectrum has y parameters, this data set contains them in the same format as described above for the xparameters dataset.

formalpara.title: The metadata dataset
formalpara.para: Contains spectrum metadata. This is stored as an even number of StrType(PredType::C_S1, H5T_VARIABLE) (variable length string) items. These items come in pairs. The first item of each pair is the name of a spetrum metadata item. The second, item of pair is the value of that item.

appendix.para: If any of this is unclear, refer to the file hdf5SpectrumReader.cpp that is installed in the $SpecTclHome/share/hdf5example of in the hdf5reader directory of the unrolled SpecTcl source tarball.
